Goldman Sachs: “Has the iPhone Entered a Super Cycle?”  Apple shares rose 4% on Monday to a record high of $262.24. With Counterpoint Research data indicating strong demand for the iPhone 17 series, speculation is spreading among investors that an iPhone super cycle has arrived.  Goldman Sachs’ latest report highlights that delivery (shipping) lead times for the newest iPhone models have been somewhat extended, emphasizing this as another sign of strong demand. Buoyed by this optimistic report, the share prices of Apple’s major supply-chain partners in Asia also rose.  According to the latest data from Counterpoint Research, sales of the iPhone 17 series in the first 10 days after launch in the U.S. and China increased by 14% compared to the same period for the iPhone 16 series. Counterpoint Senior Analyst Mengmeng Zhang wrote in the report:  “The base model of the iPhone 17 is highly attractive to consumers and offers strong value for money.”  In the report, the team led by Goldman Sachs analyst Michael Ng pointed out that demand for the iPhone 17 series could surpass that of the iPhone 16, citing as supporting evidence longer delivery lead times, higher production capacity planning, and active feedback from carriers.  “How does the demand trend for the iPhone 17 compare to previous generations? Are we entering an iPhone super cycle?” On this question, Michael Ng stated in the report:  “We believe demand for the iPhone 17 series could surpass that of the iPhone 16.”  The report cited the following evidence:  (1) Noticeably extended delivery lead times versus the 16 series; (2) An increase in total production planning; (3) Positive recent feedback from carrier channels.  Globally, during the 33 days after pre-orders began, the iPhone 17 series had an average delivery lead time of 24 days, exceeding the iPhone 16 series’ 20 days in the same period in 2024.  Base model: Lead times are distinctly longer than for the base models of the iPhone 15 and 16 Pro and Pro Max: Somewhat longer than the equivalent iPhone 16 models iPhone Air: Initially shorter than the iPhone 16 Plus, but has now flipped  By region, delivery lead times for the iPhone 17 have already surpassed those of the iPhone 16 series during the same period in the U.S., U.K., India, Japan, and Hong Kong. In mainland China, there are delays for the iPhone Air model, but lead times for the other iPhone 17 models still robustly exceed those of the prior year’s period. Goldman Sachs noted that there may be some distortion in the mainland China data. Consumers who would originally have chosen the Air model may have shifted to other iPhone 17 models, potentially leading to an overestimation of demand.  Before Apple reports earnings on October 30, Goldman Sachs analyst Michael Ng projected that iPhone sales would rise 10% year over year and Mac sales 12% year over year, leading Apple’s fiscal Q4 2025 revenue and EPS to beat expectations. The projected gross margin is 46.5%, reflecting roughly $1.1 billion in tariff costs. The report stated:  “Given the continued strength in iPhone demand, we have raised our EPS forecasts by an average of about 3% for fiscal 2025 through fiscal 2027.”  Since the iPhone 17 was announced on September 9, the strong momentum of the iPhone 17 series has triggered concurrent share-price gains among Apple’s supply-chain companies in Asia. Key suppliers that rely on Apple for more than half of their revenue—such as Luxshare Precision, LG Display, and LG Innotek—have all seen their share prices rise more than 20%. Although valuation doubts remain, the record high in Apple’s share price could keep the rally in supply-chain companies going through year-end.  According to Bloomberg, Apple’s recovery is also having a positive impact on Taiwan’s stock market. Even amid the artificial intelligence boom, TSMC and Hon Hai (Foxconn) still rely significantly on Apple-related revenue. These two giants account for as much as 47% of the Taiwan Weighted Index, making the iPhone 17’s success effectively an invisible stimulus for the Taiwan market.  That said, as the Goldman Sachs analyst emphasized, whether this marks the start of an “iPhone super cycle” remains to be seen.  $AAPL

Apple: The iPhone 17 Supercycle Is Real — And Investors Might Be Underestimating It  ( $AAPL  Rating: Hold) | By Talha Quraishi  When it comes to Apple $AAPL, skepticism always seems to arrive just before the next big leap. I’ve seen this cycle repeat countless times investors worry about iPhone fatigue, margin pressure, or China headwinds only for Apple to quietly engineer another surge in demand that resets expectations. I believe the iPhone 17 cycle could be exactly that kind of inflection point the kind that redefines what the market expects from Apple’s hardware and ecosystem growth over the next two years.  Back in June 2025, I maintained a Hold rating after the April meltdown, arguing that while iPhone momentum was soft, Apple’s cash flow strength and buyback program still provided a solid floor. Fast forward to today, and the picture has changed. The iPhone 17 launch has not only revived consumer excitement but also reignited investor confidence, pushing Apple shares up nearly 23% since the summer double the broader market’s performance.  But here’s the thing: I don’t think this is just a product rally. I think we’re witnessing the start of a meaningful upgrade cycle that could drive Apple’s next leg of earnings expansion into FY26 even as valuation and regulatory risks remind us not to lose discipline.  The iPhone 17 Isn’t Just Another Launch — It’s the Start of a Replacement Supercycle  Every major Apple cycle begins with a familiar mix of hype and doubt. The iPhone 17 is different because the demand data isn’t just strong it’s record-breaking. Early pre-orders have blown past last year’s iPhone 16 series, with China setting new records in the first minute of availability. In fact, Apple reportedly asked suppliers to ramp up daily output by 40% to meet early demand.  Even in a cautious global market, that’s a rare signal. Consumers aren’t just buying; they’re upgrading to higher-end models. The iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max are leading sales across most regions, with lead times averaging 18 to 25 days up nearly 80% year over year. Those longer waits are a bullish real-time proxy for demand, and historically, they’ve correlated closely with shipment outperformance in the following quarter.  What’s driving this rush? Several factors are converging:  ▫️ A long-overdue replacement cycle nearly 315 million users haven’t upgraded in four years.  ▫️ A noticeable step-up in hardware appeal, from the A19 chip’s performance to the improved battery life and camera upgrades that genuinely separate the Pro line from competitors like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 7.  ▫️ Government subsidies in China that favor the base iPhone 17 model, helping Apple defend market share despite Huawei’s resurgence.  It’s also worth noting that Apple has strategically extended support cycles while ending compatibility for older devices. The iOS 26.0.1 update no longer supports the iPhone X series, subtly encouraging faster upgrade behavior. For a company whose ecosystem thrives on installed-base growth, this matters a lot.  A Rare Sweet Spot: High ASPs, Strong Mix, and Expanding Installed Base  The bullish setup for FY26 is not just about units it’s about mix and monetization. Evercore ISI data shows that 56% of surveyed buyers plan to purchase Pro models, which command premium pricing and higher margins. Even if average selling prices (ASPs) tick slightly lower (estimated at $1,053 for December 2025, down marginally from last year), volume growth and richer configurations more than offset the dip.  JP Morgan’s latest forecast calls for 236 million iPhone shipments in FY26, up 2% YoY not a massive number, but with a stronger Pro mix, it translates into an estimated $80 billion in iPhone revenue. That’s crucial, because hardware strength feeds directly into Apple’s services engine, which now contributes over 25% of total revenue with 70%+ gross margins.  In my view, this is Apple’s hidden flywheel: the more iPhones in circulation, the more Apple can monetize through App Store fees, iCloud subscriptions, and now, emerging AI-driven services. Even small incremental shifts in the installed base compound into billions in recurring revenue over time.  India and Diversification: Apple’s Quiet Hedge Against Tariffs  While the tariff headlines have spooked parts of the market, I think investors are missing how quickly Apple is diversifying production. The company now manufactures all iPhone 17 models in India, exporting roughly $7.5 billion worth of devices in just four months up sharply from last year’s full-year total of $17 billion.  This shift isn’t cosmetic. It’s a structural de-risking move that mitigates Apple’s China dependency and softens the blow from U.S.-China tariff tensions. With Hon Hai Precision (Foxconn) expanding operations in both India and Vietnam, Apple’s supply chain is becoming more resilient.  Still, I’m watching margins closely. In Q3 FY25, Apple’s product gross margin slipped to 34.5% down 1.4 percentage points sequentially partly due to cost pressures and early tariff provisions. Management guided for up to $1.1 billion in tariff impact for Q4 FY25. If Apple can offset even part of that through geographic diversification and operational efficiency, it will reinforce confidence in the company’s ability to protect profitability despite external headwinds.  Valuation: Still Expensive, But Not Unreasonable for a Quality Compounder  Let’s talk valuation because it’s the biggest question I get from investors right now. Yes, Apple looks pricey at a forward P/E of roughly 33x, above its 5-year average of 28.6x and its 10-year average near 22x. But when I compare that to the broader Magnificent 7 group (average P/E of ~31x), Apple’s premium doesn’t seem excessive especially given its balance sheet strength, massive buyback program, and stable cash flows.  To me, the more telling metric is the PEG ratio. At 3.3x, Apple’s valuation implies the market is paying up for consistent growth, not hypergrowth. That’s justified if the iPhone 17 cycle drives even mid-single-digit earnings acceleration in FY26, followed by continued Services expansion.  In other words, the stock isn’t cheap, but quality rarely is. And in a volatile tech market where AI narratives dominate headlines, Apple’s story of disciplined execution and ecosystem monetization still commands a premium for good reason.  The Elephant in the Room: Regulation and AI Execution  No Apple thesis is complete without addressing the regulatory and AI overhang. The European Commission’s €500 million fine earlier this year for Digital Markets Act violations is just one symptom of broader scrutiny. Apple is being pushed to loosen its App Store rules a change that could shave a few hundred million from annual service revenue.  Meanwhile, the company’s AI rollout has been slower than rivals’. Siri’s next major update has reportedly been delayed to 2026, with talent departures (including six key engineers to Meta since July) hinting at internal turbulence. That said, Apple’s pragmatic approach integrating OpenAI’s ChatGPT into iOS while maintaining privacy-first architecture could prove smarter over time than rushing half-baked AI models to market.  Regulatory risks are real, but manageable. Even under stricter DMA rules, Apple’s ecosystem lock-in remains extraordinarily strong. Developers and users may complain about Apple’s control, but few are leaving the platform.  The Bigger Picture: Why I’m Staying Slightly Bullish  When I zoom out, the iPhone 17 cycle feels less like a one-off sales bump and more like a structural reset one that could anchor the next phase of Apple’s earnings story. Here’s why I believe the market is still underestimating it:  1.  A powerful upgrade base: 300+ million users are overdue for a new device.  2.  Premium model dominance: The Pro and Pro Max mix boosts margins even in a flat unit environment.  3.  Services compounding: Every hardware sale fuels higher-margin digital revenue streams.  4.  Geographic hedging: India’s rise in Apple’s supply chain will help cushion geopolitical risks.  4.  Capital efficiency: With one of the largest buyback programs in corporate history, Apple keeps amplifying shareholder returns.  Yes, valuation is stretched. Yes, regulatory friction is rising. But when I weigh those risks against Apple’s operating leverage, balance sheet resilience, and brand stickiness, I still find it hard to bet against the company at this stage of the cycle.  My Takeaway  I’m maintaining a slightly bullish stance on Apple going into the October 30 FQ4’25 earnings call. I believe the iPhone 17 supercycle will drive upside surprises in both unit sales and gross margins through FY26, with services providing a durable earnings floor.  At current levels around 33x forward earnings, I wouldn’t call Apple cheap but I also wouldn’t fade it. For long-term investors, especially those looking beyond the next quarter, I see this as an opportunity to accumulate gradually on dips rather than chase the momentum.  Apple has a history of proving doubters wrong. And if the iPhone 17 momentum holds through the holiday quarter, I wouldn’t be surprised to see Wall Street recalibrate its expectations again this time, to the upside.

No, the majority of iPhones in Nigeria are not fake. What you mostly find are foreign-used or refurbished iPhones rather than counterfeit devices. Refurbished phones are genuine Apple products that have been repaired or restored to good working condition, often by authorized service providers or reputable sellers. This is quite common in many countries where brand-new devices might be expensive or less accessible.  If you want to verify the authenticity of any Apple product, you can easily do so by visiting https://t.co/3twbj7u5QJ and entering the device’s serial number. This will confirm whether the device is genuine and provide warranty and support information directly from Apple.  Apple manufactures iPhones with different model numbers tailored for specific regions around the world. This is due to variations in cellular bands, regulatory requirements, and sometimes software features that differ by country or region.  For example, the iPhone 17 comes in several regional versions such as:  •A3526 for International markets •A3257 for the USA •A3525 for the Middle East, Canada, and Mexico •A3527 for China  All these models are 100% original Apple products, but they’re optimized to work best in their respective regions. This means that an iPhone designed for the US market might support different network bands or have slight hardware differences compared to one made for China or Europe. However, none of these regional differences imply that any version is fake or inferior.  It makes sense that official Apple Stores in the US primarily sell the US-specific iPhone models (like A3257) because they are designed to serve the US market’s network standards and regulations. Due to high demand, especially for new flagship models like the iPhone 17, it’s common for these stores to run out of stock quickly.  This does not mean that iPhones available in Nigeria are fake just because the official Apple Store in the US is sold out. Many iPhones in Nigeria come through importers who bring in new, foreign-used, or refurbished devices from various regions.  Okay, bye. ✌🏽
